newsitem.title: USA: NYC official seeks US group to monitor Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: NYC official seeks US group to monitor Swiss banks.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi proposed Wednesday that an ad hoc group of U.S. public officials, including state treasurers, and public pension funds monitor Swiss banks in the wake of allegations that Swiss banks hoarded unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims.
"I think it will be useful to exchange this information," Hevesi said at a press conference here in his offices.

"We're not interested in applying pressure, we're interested in encouraging the Swiss to continue on a path that is positive," Hevesi said. Last week he went to Switzerland where he met Swiss Bank and government officials and Jewish leaders.
Saying a coordinated approach was needed, Hevesi said: "We will be monitoring this and our relationship will be a function of their producing what they promised."

While he made it plain that whether or not the Swiss banks are allowed to keep doing "substantial" business with the city depends on how they treat Holocaust victims, Hevesi stopped short of punitive steps.
"We're not ready to participate in a boycott. We want to encourage the Swiss to do the right thing," he said.

The three Swiss banks with whom the city comptroller met were CS Group, Union Bank of Switzerland and Swiss Bank Corp. Hevesi is a trustee and investment advisor for the city's $70 billion pension fund, which owned 322,880 shares--a $47.6 million stake--in the three banks, as of December 31, 1996. The banks also handle some of the city's short-term deposits.

Hevesi, who said he might contact state comptrollers and private pension funds as part of his effort to set up an ad hoc monitoring group, added that he was both encourged and disappointed by the latest developments in Switzerland.

The Swiss banks said they would be prepared to publish a list of dormant accounts by name and account number and make them available in Switzerland, Europe, Israel and the United States, as well as hand any unclaimed accounts to the government.
But Hevesi warned that the Solidarity Fund proposed by the Swiss government might never be enacted.
"The fund must be approved by a referendum and virtually every government official, community leader and banker I spoke to thought that approval would be difficult," he said.

The Solidarity Fund would get its money from an extra seven billion of Swiss francs produced by revaluing gold reserves. But Hevesi faulted the plan, saying only the interest generated -- about 400 million Swiss francs a year -- would be available for aid, adding that there was no assurance Holocaust victims would get funds. The Solidarity Fund has a broad aim of helping victims of poverty, oppression and disasters, both in Switzerland and abroad.
